newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO warns of "explosion", calls for confrontation.
newsitem.headline: PLO warns of "explosion", calls for confrontation.

text.p: The PLO, warning that hardline Israeli policies were leading the Middle East to the brink of an explosion, urged Palestinians to "confront with all possible means" plans to expand Jewish settlements.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's cabinet met in Gaza late on Friday, hours after the Israeli government agreed to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the West Bank, a move the PLO said was a decision to kill off the peace process.

The incentives, which could entice more Israelis to settle in the occupied area, were seen as a strong sign of defiance by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to world opposition to his plans to tighten Israel's hold on captured Arab land.
"Israel's measures aim at destroying the peace process and leading the whole region to the edge of an explosion," said a statement released after the Palestinian cabinet meeting.

The PLO statement condemned plans to expand existing Jewish settlements, the Friday decision on incentives, and Israel's deployment of tanks in response to Israeli-PLO gun battles that cost scores of lives in September.
"The Palestinian leadership calls on the masses everywhere to firmly confront with all possible means the Israeli settlement aggression in order to defend the land," it said.
Late on Friday the Israeli army said Katyusha rockets slammed into the Western Galilee area of northern Israel.

The salvo was the first such attack on the area since a U.S. brokered ceasefire ended a 17-day Israeli blitz against rocket-firing Hizbollah guerrillas in April. The pro-Iranian Hizbollah denied responsibility for the Friday barrage.
The army added that a petrol bomb set afire an Israeli army patrol truck near a Druze Arab town late on Friday in the occupied Golan Heights. No injuries were reported in the attack.

At its weekly meeting, Netanyahu's cabinet decided to reinstate benefits for West Bank settlers, such as lower taxes, that are already given to residents of disadvantaged towns inside Israel, and to Israelis in Gaza and the Golan Heights.
The move came two days after radical Palestinian gunmen killed a settler and her 12-year-old son in a drive-by shooting near PLO-ruled Ramallah.

Israel's main ally Washington, going beyond standard U.S. phraseology, called the settlement incentive decision "troubling", suggesting it could hamper peace talks as a step "seen to pre-empt the outcome of a negotiation."

The fate of settlements, in which more than 130,000 Jews live among the two million Arabs of the West Bank and Gaza, is to be decided in "final status" talks on the thorniest disputes between Israel and the PLO.
The talks have been shelved, however, as the sides wrangle over still-unresolved interim issues such as a long-delayed Israeli pullout from the West Bank flashpoint of Hebron.

Since taking office in June, the Netanyahu government has given the go-ahead for the construction of thousands of homes in existing settlements but has yet to meet the demands of settler leaders to establish new outposts.
Palestinians fear Netanyahu's government is creating "facts on the ground" to cement its control over Arab land.
Senior Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters:

"To consider the West Bank as part of Israel and to expand and encourage settlements means Netanyahu is officially killing the peace process, which was based on the crucial principle of gradually ending occupation."

Under the landmark 1993 peace deal with the PLO, Israel's previous Labour government withdrew from much of the Gaza Strip and from most Palestinian towns in the West Bank. But Netanyahu has pledged to bolster Jewish settlements, long seen by Arabs and Washington as a main obstacle to peace.
In Damascus, radical Palestinian leader George Habash, 71, pledged more attacks on Israelis and urged Palestinians to launch a fresh uprising against the Jewish state.
Habash's Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine claimed responsibity for the Wednesday ambush killing of a Jewish settler and her 12-year-old son in the West Bank.
The militant Moslem Hamas group also vowed to attack Israelis to mark the January anniversary of the killing of the group's master bombmaker, reportedly at the hands of Israel.
